content: Pompe disease is a genetic disorder caused by a deficiency of the enzyme acid alpha-glucosidase (GAA). In individuals with infantile-onset Pompe disease, there is either a complete or near-complete lack of this enzyme. In contrast, those with late-onset Pompe disease (LOPD) retain some residual GAA activity. The treatment for GAA deficiency involves enzyme replacement therapy (ERT), which is administered through intravenous infusions of recombinant human acid alglucosidase alfa. Currently, alglucosidase alfa and avalglucosidase alfa are approved treatments for Pompe disease, while cipaglucosidase alfa combined with miglustat has not yet received approval. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the effects of ERT in individuals with LOPD. The authors conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, clinical trial registries, and reference lists of relevant articles, with the last search performed on April 21, 2022. They included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving participants of any age with LOPD. Two reviewers independently assessed the eligibility of trials, extracted data, and evaluated the risk of bias and the certainty of evidence using the GRADE approach. Disagreements were resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer. Six trials involving 358 participants were included, with study durations ranging from 12 to 78 weeks. The trials assessed various comparisons, but none evaluated two secondary outcomes: the need for respiratory support and the use of walking aids or wheelchairs. The certainty of evidence was often downgraded due to selective reporting bias. 1. Alglucosidase alfa versus placebo (90 participants): After 78 weeks, alglucosidase alfa likely improves the six-minute walk test (6MWT) distance compared to placebo, with a mean difference (MD) of 30.95 meters (95% confidence interval [CI] 7.98 to 53.92; moderate-certainty evidence). It also likely improves respiratory function, as measured by the change in percent predicted forced vital capacity (FVC), with an MD of 3.55% (95% CI 1.46 to 5.64; moderate-certainty evidence). There may be little or no difference between the groups in the occurrence of infusion reactions (risk ratio [RR] 1.21, 95% CI 0.57 to 2.61; low-certainty evidence), quality of life physical component scores (MD -1.36 points, 95% CI -5.59 to 2.87; low-certainty evidence), or adverse events (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.64 to 1.39; low-certainty evidence). 2. Alglucosidase alfa plus clenbuterol versus alglucosidase alfa plus placebo (13 participants): The evidence is very uncertain regarding the effect of adding clenbuterol to alglucosidase alfa on the 6MWT distance after 52 weeks (MD 34.55 meters, 95% CI -10.11 to 79.21; very low-certainty evidence) and the change in percent predicted FVC (MD -13.51%, 95% CI -32.44 to 5.41; very low-certainty evidence). This study did not assess infusion reactions, quality of life, or adverse events. 3. Alglucosidase alfa plus albuterol versus alglucosidase alfa plus placebo (13 participants): The evidence is very uncertain about the effect of adding albuterol to alglucosidase alfa on the 6MWT distance after 52 weeks (MD 30.00 meters, 95% CI 0.55 to 59.45; very low-certainty evidence), the change in percent predicted FVC (MD -4.30%, 95% CI -14.87 to 6.27; very low-certainty evidence), and the risk of adverse events (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.38 to 1.18; very low-certainty evidence). This study did not measure infusion reactions or quality of life. 4. VAL-1221 versus alglucosidase alfa (12 participants): Insufficient data were available to estimate the effects of VAL-1221 compared to alglucosidase alfa at one year or later. At three months, VAL-1221 may increase or decrease infusion-associated reactions compared to alglucosidase alfa, but the evidence is very uncertain (RR 2.80, 95% CI 0.18 to 42.80). This study did not assess quality of life or adverse events. 5. Cipaglucosidase alfa plus miglustat versus alglucosidase alfa plus placebo (125 participants): Compared to alglucosidase alfa plus placebo, cipaglucosidase alfa plus miglustat may result in little or no difference in the 6MWT distance at 52 weeks (MD 13.60 meters, 95% CI -2.26 to 29.46; low-certainty evidence), infusion reactions (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.49 to 1.80; low-certainty evidence), quality of life scores for physical function (MD 1.70, 95% CI -2.13 to 5.53; low-certainty evidence) and fatigue (MD -0.30, 95% CI -2.76 to 2.16; low-certainty evidence), or adverse events potentially related to treatment (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.49 to 1.40; low-certainty evidence). However, cipaglucosidase alfa plus miglustat likely improves percent predicted FVC compared to alglucosidase alfa plus placebo (MD 3.10%, 95% CI 1.04 to 5.16; moderate-certainty evidence). It may make little or no difference in percent predicted sniff nasal inspiratory pressure (MD -0.06%, 95% CI -8.91 to 7.71; low-certainty evidence). 6. Avalglucosidase alfa versus alglucosidase alfa (100 participants): After 49 weeks, avalglucosidase alfa likely improves the 6MWT distance compared to alglucosidase alfa (MD 30.02 meters, 95% CI 1.84 to 58.20; moderate-certainty evidence). It likely results in little or no difference in percent predicted FVC compared to alglucosidase alfa (MD 2.43%, 95% CI -0.08 to 4.94; moderate-certainty evidence). Avalglucosidase alfa may result in little or no difference in infusion reactions (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.42 to 1.45; low-certainty evidence), quality of life (MD 0.77, 95% CI -2.09 to 3.63; low-certainty evidence), or treatment-related adverse events (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.61 to 1.40; low-certainty evidence). In conclusion, one trial demonstrated that alglucosidase alfa likely improves the 6MWT distance and respiratory function compared to placebo. Avalglucosidase alfa likely improves the 6MWT distance compared to alglucosidase alfa. Cipaglucosidase alfa plus miglustat likely improves FVC compared to alglucosidase alfa plus placebo. Trials investigating the addition of clenbuterol or albuterol to alglucosidase alfa provided little to no evidence of benefit. No significant increase in adverse events was observed with any of the ERTs. However, the impact of ERT on certain outcomes remains unclear, and longer RCTs are needed to provide more robust data due to the progressive nature of LOPD. Post-marketing registries may also help capture additional information.
